definition: The study of how much time, memory or other resources a problem needs as its input grows. Where computability asks whether an algorithm exists at all, complexity theory asks whether an efficient one does.
example: Complexity theory explains why shortest paths are easy but finding the shortest tour through every city appears not to be.

definition: A set of problems that can be solved within a stated resource limit on a stated kind of machine, such as "decision problems solvable in polynomial time on a deterministic machine" (the class P).
example: P, NP, PSPACE and BQP are all complexity classes.

definition: A problem whose answer is just yes or no for each input. Complexity classes such as P and NP are defined for decision problems; an optimisation problem is usually turned into one by asking "is there a solution of cost at most k?".
example: "Does this graph have a route of length at most 100?" is a decision problem; "find the shortest route" is not.

definition: A set of strings over a fixed alphabet. In complexity theory a decision problem is identified with the language of inputs whose answer is yes, so "x is in L" means "x is a yes-instance".
example: The language SAT is the set of all Boolean formulas, written as strings, that have a satisfying assignment.

definition: One specific input to a problem. The problem "is this graph 3-colourable?" has one instance per possible graph.
example: A particular 50-city map with a budget of 1,000 km is one instance of the travelling salesman decision problem.

definition: For a decision problem, a yes-instance is an input whose correct answer is yes, and a no-instance is one whose answer is no. NP is about short proofs for yes-instances; coNP about short proofs for no-instances.
example: A satisfiable formula is a yes-instance of SAT; an unsatisfiable one is a no-instance.

definition: The length of an input, written n: characters for a string, elements for a list or, in complexity theory, bits in a reasonable encoding. Running times are stated as functions of n; in complexity theory a number N counts as about log₂ N bits, not N.
example: The number 1,000,000 has an input size of 20 bits.

definition: The largest time or space cost over inputs of a fixed size. Deterministic worst-case bounds constrain every such input; expected-time and randomised error bounds additionally state how costs or errors are averaged over an algorithm’s own randomness.
example: Quicksort with a naive pivot is O(n²) in the worst case even though it is usually much faster.

definition: Describing how a cost grows for large inputs while ignoring constant factors and small inputs. Big O, Big Omega and Big Theta are its standard notations.
example: 3n² + 5n and 100n² are both asymptotically n²: both are O(n²).

definition: Notation for an asymptotic lower bound: f(n) = Ω(g(n)) means f eventually grows at least as fast as a constant times g(n). It is used to say that something needs at least a certain amount of work.
example: Grover-style black-box search needs Ω(√N) queries: no quantum algorithm can do it with fewer, up to a constant factor.

definition: Notation for a strictly smaller growth rate: f(n) = o(g(n)) means f(n)/g(n) tends to 0 as n grows. It is stronger than Big O, which allows equal growth.
example: log n = o(n), and n = o(n²), but n is not o(2n).

definition: The class of decision problems that a deterministic algorithm can solve in polynomial time: at most about n^k steps on an n-bit input, for some fixed k. It is the standard formal meaning of "efficiently solvable".
example: Decision versions of shortest paths, 2-SAT, rational linear programming and primality testing are all in P.

definition: Running time that grows like 2 to the power of a polynomial in n, such as 2ⁿ. Each extra bit of input can double the work, so exponential algorithms become hopeless quickly.
example: At n = 100, 2ⁿ is about 1.3 × 10³⁰ steps, far beyond any computer.

definition: A time bound of two raised to a fixed power of the logarithm of input length. The representative function is polynomial when that power is one and grows faster than every polynomial when the power exceeds one; an upper bound of this form does not itself prove an algorithm needs super-polynomial time.
example: Babai showed graph isomorphism can be solved in quasi-polynomial time (2015, corrected 2017).

definition: A running-time bound of two raised to an exponent that grows more slowly than linearly in the input bit length; this is the convention used in the Exponential Time Hypothesis. Another, stronger convention requires a bound smaller than two raised to every positive power of the input length, so always state the convention. The general number field sieve has a heuristic expected subexponential bound in the first sense, not that stronger sense.
example: The general number field sieve has a heuristic expected estimate roughly exp(c (ln N)^(1/3) (ln ln N)^(2/3)) for a constant c.

definition: A running-time bound polynomial in numeric input values rather than their binary encoding lengths. A positive integer written in b bits is smaller than two to the power b, so such a table-filling algorithm can take exponentially many operations in the encoded input length.
example: Subset sum's O(n·T) dynamic program is pseudo-polynomial: a 64-bit target T can be about 1.8 × 10¹⁹.

definition: An algorithm (or machine) whose next step is completely fixed by its current state and input: no guessing and no random choices. P and SPACE classes are defined with deterministic machines.
example: Ordinary programs without random-number calls are deterministic: the same input always gives the same run.

definition: A Turing machine that may have several possible next moves and accepts if any sequence of choices leads to acceptance. It can be pictured as "guessing" correctly; NP is exactly what such a machine decides in polynomial time.
example: To decide SAT nondeterministically, guess a value for each variable, then check the formula.

definition: An abstract computer with indexed memory whose arithmetic instructions act on explicitly bounded words, rather than arbitrary integers at unit cost. With polynomially bounded word lengths and suitable operation costs, this classical model and Turing machines simulate each other with polynomial overhead.
example: Algorithm textbooks usually count steps on a RAM machine.

definition: The unproven claim that any physically realisable computer can be simulated by a probabilistic Turing machine with at most polynomial slowdown. Quantum computers are the main challenge to it, since factoring is efficient for them but not known to be for classical machines.

Nondeterministic polynomial time: the decision problems whose yes-instances have a certificate of polynomial length that a deterministic algorithm can check in polynomial time. Every problem in P is also in NP; "NP" does not mean "not polynomial".
example: SAT is in NP: a satisfying assignment is a certificate, checked by evaluating the formula.

definition: The class of decision problems whose complement is in NP: every no-instance has a short certificate checkable in polynomial time. Whether coNP equals NP is open and believed false.
example: UNSAT ("this formula has no satisfying assignment") and TAUTOLOGY are coNP-complete.

definition: Evidence for a stated answer that a verifier can check. In NP, every yes-instance has a polynomial-size certificate checked in polynomial time; a no-certificate instead supports a no-answer, as in coNP. Finding such evidence may be harder than checking it.
example: For subset sum, the certificate is the chosen subset; checking it is one addition per element.

definition: An algorithm V(x, c) that takes an input x and a proposed certificate c and accepts or rejects. A problem is in NP when a polynomial-time verifier accepts some certificate exactly for the yes-instances.
example: A SAT verifier plugs the proposed assignment into the formula and checks every clause is true.

definition: The property of being NP-hard: every problem in NP reduces to the problem in polynomial time. If P ≠ NP, an NP-hard problem has no polynomial-time algorithm that works on every input.

The property of being NP-complete: the problem is in NP and every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time. NP-complete problems are the hardest problems in NP; a fast algorithm for any one would give fast algorithms for all of NP.
example: Cook and Levin proved SAT NP-complete; Karp extended it to 21 more problems in 1972.

definition: A weakly NP-complete numeric decision problem, such as subset sum, has a pseudo-polynomial algorithm that becomes polynomial when its numeric values are polynomially bounded in the encoded input length. Strong NP-completeness means hardness remains under polynomial numeric bounds; 3-partition and TSP decision with weights one or two illustrate this.
example: Subset sum and knapsack are weakly NP-complete; 3-partition and TSP are strongly NP-complete.

definition: Problems in NP that are neither in P nor NP-complete. Ladner's theorem shows they exist if P ≠ NP; factoring and graph isomorphism are natural candidates, but none can be proved intermediate without proving P ≠ NP.
A 1975 result of Richard Ladner: if P ≠ NP, then NP contains problems that are neither in P nor NP-complete. The problems it constructs are artificial.

The open question of whether every problem whose solutions can be checked quickly (NP) can also be solved quickly (P). Almost all experts believe P ≠ NP; it is one of the Clay Millennium Prize problems, with a $1 million prize.
Seven mathematical problems for which the Clay Mathematics Institute offered $1 million each in 2000. P vs NP is one; only the Poincaré conjecture has been solved.
A theorem (Hartmanis and Stearns, 1965) that, given substantially more time, a deterministic machine can solve strictly more problems. It proves, for example, that P ≠ EXPTIME.

A theorem that machines with substantially more memory can decide strictly more problems: SPACE(s) is strictly inside SPACE(s′) when s grows strictly more slowly than s′ (for well-behaved s′ ≥ log n). It proves NL ≠ PSPACE and PSPACE ≠ EXPSPACE.

A class is closed under complement if, whenever a problem is in it, the problem with yes and no swapped is too. P is closed under complement (flip the output); whether NP is, is the NP vs coNP question.
example: The complement of SAT is UNSAT.

definition: The class of decision problems solvable by a deterministic machine in time 2 to the power of a polynomial in n. It contains P, NP and PSPACE, and by the time hierarchy theorem strictly contains P.
example: Deciding who wins generalised chess on an n × n board is EXPTIME-complete.

definition: Nondeterministic exponential time: decision problems a nondeterministic machine decides in time 2 to the power of a polynomial. It is the exponential-time analogue of NP.

The class of decision problems solvable using an amount of memory polynomial in the input size, with no explicit time bound but still required to halt. It contains NP and coNP, and is contained in EXPTIME.
example: TQBF and generalised geography are PSPACE-complete.

definition: Problems decidable by a nondeterministic machine in polynomial space. Savitch's theorem shows NPSPACE = PSPACE: for memory, nondeterminism adds nothing at polynomial scale.
Problems decidable using exponential memory: 2 to the power of a polynomial in n. By the space hierarchy theorem it strictly contains PSPACE.
example: Equivalence of regular expressions extended with a squaring operator is EXPSPACE-complete.

definition: The class L: decision problems a deterministic machine solves using O(log n) cells of work memory, enough for a fixed number of counters or pointers into the read-only input.
example: Reachability in undirected graphs is in L (Reingold, 2005).

definition: Nondeterministic logarithmic space: decision problems a nondeterministic machine solves with O(log n) work memory. Directed reachability (PATH) is NL-complete; whether L = NL is open.
The complements of NL problems. The Immerman–Szelepcsényi theorem proves NL = coNL, so a log-space nondeterministic machine can also certify unreachability.
The class of decision problems a deterministic machine decides using O(s(n)) cells of work tape on inputs of length n. L is SPACE(log n) and PSPACE is the union of SPACE(n^k).
The class of decision problems a nondeterministic machine decides using O(s(n)) work cells. coNSPACE(s) holds their complements; Immerman–Szelepcsényi shows the two are equal for s ≥ log n.
The class of decision problems a deterministic machine decides in O(t(n)) steps on inputs of length n. P is the union of TIME(n^k) over all fixed k.
The amount of working memory an algorithm or machine needs, as a function of input size. Unlike time, memory can be reused, which is why space classes behave differently from time classes.
example: Savitch's reachability algorithm uses O(log² n) space but n^O(log n) time.

definition: The number of basic steps an algorithm takes, as a function of the input size n, usually stated with Big O for the worst case.

In space-bounded Turing machines, a tape holding the input that can be read but not written. Only the separate work tape counts towards the space used, which makes sublinear (e.g. logarithmic) space meaningful.
The read/write tape a space-bounded Turing machine uses as scratch memory. Space complexity counts only the work-tape cells used.

Working space that grows strictly more slowly than the input length: its ratio to that length tends to zero, as with logarithmic space. The standard model keeps read-only input separate from counted working memory.
example: A log-space algorithm on a 1 GB input might keep only a few 64-bit counters.

definition: A complete snapshot of a machine at one moment: its control state, its head positions and the contents of its work tape. A run is a sequence of configurations, one per step.
example: A machine using s cells has about n · s · |Γ|^s · |Q| configurations, which is 2^O(s) for s ≥ log n.

definition: A directed graph with one vertex per possible configuration of a machine on an input and an edge for each legal single step. Acceptance becomes reachability from the start configuration to an accepting one.
The rule table of an automaton or Turing machine: for each state and symbol read, it gives the next state, the symbol to write and the head move (or several options, if nondeterministic).

A polynomial-time function f that turns every instance x of problem A into an instance f(x) of problem B with the same yes/no answer, written A ≤_p B. It shows B is at least as hard as A: a fast algorithm for B would give one for A.
example: Setting k = number of clauses and drawing one triangle per clause reduces 3-SAT to Independent Set.

definition: A reduction that solves A using an algorithm for B as a subroutine that may be called many times, with the answers post-processed. It is more powerful than a many-one reduction; for example SAT and UNSAT reduce to each other trivially this way.
A reduction computed by a machine using only O(log n) work memory. It is the standard reduction for classes inside P, such as NL, where polynomial-time reductions would be too strong.
example: PATH is NL-complete under log-space reductions.

definition: A small piece of the target problem built to imitate one part of the source problem, such as a variable ("choose true or false") or a clause ("at least one of these holds"). Reductions are assembled from gadgets.
example: In 3-SAT to Independent Set, each clause becomes a triangle gadget: an independent set can take at most one of its three vertices.

definition: In the 3-SAT to Independent Set reduction, edges joining every vertex labelled x to every vertex labelled ¬x, so an independent set can never pick a variable and its negation together.

The theorem (Cook 1971; Levin independently, published 1973) that SAT is NP-complete. It encodes any polynomial-time nondeterministic computation as a Boolean formula that is satisfiable exactly when the computation can accept.

In the Cook–Levin proof, a grid whose rows are the successive configurations of a machine's run, one row per step. For a run of n^k steps it is n^k by n^k cells, so the formula describing it has polynomial size.
example: A cubic-time machine on a 100-symbol input gives a tableau of 10⁶ × 10⁶ = 10¹² cells.

definition: A 2-by-3 block of adjacent cells in the Cook–Levin tableau. Because a Turing machine only changes cells next to its head in one step, checking that every window is legal is enough to check the whole run.
A decision problem that no algorithm can solve correctly on every input, such as the halting problem. Undecidable problems can still be NP-hard, but they are not in NP.
The problem of deciding whether a Boolean formula has an assignment of true/false values to its variables that makes it true. It was the first problem proved NP-complete (Cook–Levin).
example: (x ∨ y) ∧ (¬x ∨ ¬y) is satisfiable: x true, y false works.

definition: SAT restricted to CNF formulas in which every clause has exactly three literals (at most three in some treatments). It is NP-complete and the usual starting point for reductions because its shape is rigid.
example: (x1 ∨ x2 ∨ ¬x3) ∧ (¬x1 ∨ x3 ∨ x4) is a 3-SAT instance.

definition: SAT restricted to clauses of two literals. Unlike 3-SAT it is in P: each clause becomes two implications, and the formula is unsatisfiable exactly when some variable and its negation reach each other in the implication graph, which takes linear time to check.

The optimisation problem of maximising the number of satisfied clauses in a 3-CNF formula. With three distinct variables per clause, a random assignment satisfies seven eighths in expectation; conditional expectation makes this a deterministic guarantee. Guaranteeing a fraction of the optimum above seven eighths by any fixed positive margin is NP-hard.
The problem of deciding that a Boolean formula has no satisfying assignment, the complement of SAT. It is coNP-complete; no short certificate of unsatisfiability is known in general.
example: x ∧ ¬x is unsatisfiable.

definition: The problem of deciding whether a Boolean formula is true under every assignment. It is coNP-complete: φ is a tautology exactly when ¬φ is unsatisfiable.
example: x ∨ ¬x is a tautology.

definition: A choice of true or false for every variable that makes a Boolean formula true. A formula with at least one is satisfiable; for SAT it serves as the certificate.
example: x1 = true, x2 = false, x3 = true satisfies (x1 ∨ x2 ∨ ¬x3) ∧ (¬x1 ∨ x3 ∨ x4).

definition: An expression built from true/false variables with AND (∧), OR (∨) and NOT (¬). SAT asks whether one can be made true.
example: (x ∨ y) ∧ ¬z is a Boolean formula in three variables.

definition: A Boolean formula written as an AND of clauses, each clause an OR of literals. 3-CNF means every clause has three literals. Many practical SAT solvers accept CNF input.
example: (x ∨ ¬y) ∧ (¬x ∨ y ∨ z) is in CNF.

definition: In a CNF formula, one bracketed OR of literals, such as (x1 ∨ ¬x2 ∨ x3). A clause is true when at least one of its literals is true, and the whole formula needs every clause true.
A Boolean variable or its negation, such as x or ¬x. Clauses are ORs of literals.
example: The clause (x1 ∨ x2 ∨ ¬x3) has three literals.

definition: A clause with at most one positive (un-negated) literal. Satisfiability of formulas made only of Horn clauses can be decided in linear time, so Horn-SAT is in P.
example: (¬x ∨ ¬y ∨ z), meaning "x and y imply z", is a Horn clause.

definition: A directed graph used to solve 2-SAT: one vertex per literal, and for each clause (a ∨ b) the arrows ¬a → b and ¬b → a. The formula is unsatisfiable exactly when some x and ¬x lie in the same strongly connected component.
A maximal group of vertices in a directed graph where every vertex can reach every other. All strongly connected components can be computed in time linear in vertices plus edges.
A new variable introduced by a construction that appears nowhere else in the formula. Clause splitting in SAT to 3-SAT uses fresh variables to chain the pieces together.
example: Splitting a 5-literal clause into three 3-literal clauses adds 2 fresh variables.

definition: A program that decides satisfiability of CNF formulas. Modern ones use conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL): search, and when a conflict occurs, learn a new clause that rules it out. They solve many large industrial instances despite NP-completeness, with performance strongly dependent on structure.
example: MiniSat, CaDiCaL and Kissat are well-known CDCL SAT solvers.

definition: A proof that a CNF formula is unsatisfiable, built by repeatedly combining two clauses that contain x and ¬x into one without them, until the empty clause appears. For some formulas, such as pigeonhole formulas, every resolution proof is exponentially long (Haken, 1985).

A standard file format in which SAT solvers record a proof that a formula is unsatisfiable, so an independent checker can verify the "no" answer. The check is polynomial in the proof's length, but the proof can be very long.
A small, influential open-source CDCL SAT solver by Eén and Sörensson (2003), widely used as a base for research solvers.

Open-source CDCL SAT solvers developed by Armin Biere and collaborators. Kissat’s documented competition results include the 2020 main-track win and the three 2024 main-track categories; such rankings are dated results rather than a universal performance ordering.
An open-source library that resolves software package dependencies by encoding them as a SAT problem. It is used by openSUSE's zypper and Fedora's dnf.
The command-line package managers of openSUSE (zypper) and Fedora/Red Hat (dnf). Both use libsolv to work out which package versions can be installed together.
Given a list of nonnegative integers and a target T, decide whether some subset adds up to exactly T. It is (weakly) NP-complete, with a pseudo-polynomial O(n·T) dynamic program.
Choose items, each with a weight and a value, to maximise total value without exceeding a weight capacity. Its decision version is weakly NP-complete; a pseudo-polynomial DP and an FPTAS exist.

Decide whether a multiset of 3m integers can be split into m triples with equal sums. It stays NP-complete even when the numbers are small (polynomial in the input size), so it is strongly NP-complete.
A set of vertices in a graph with no edge between any two of them. The Independent Set problem asks whether a graph has one of size k; it is NP-complete.
example: In the path 1–2–3, {1, 3} is an independent set.

definition: A set of vertices that touches every edge of a graph. S is an independent set exactly when the remaining vertices form a vertex cover. Deciding whether a cover of size k exists is NP-complete; a simple 2-approximation exists.
example: In the path 1–2–3–4, {2, 3} is a minimum vertex cover.

definition: A set of graph vertices all joined to one another. The decision problem is NP-complete when the requested size k is part of the input and W[1]-hard when parameterised by k. For each separately fixed k, enumeration is polynomial, with an exponent depending on k.
example: A triangle is a 3-clique.

definition: Given a universe of elements and a family of subsets, choose the fewest subsets whose union is the universe. The decision version asks whether at most k subsets suffice and is NP-complete; unweighted greedy set cover has a logarithmic approximation guarantee in the universe size.
The graph on the same vertices with an edge exactly where the original has none, written Ḡ. A set is independent in G exactly when it is a clique in Ḡ.
example: The complement of the path 1–2–3 has the single edge 1–3.

definition: Decide whether a graph's vertices can be coloured with 3 colours so that no edge joins two vertices of the same colour. It is NP-complete, while 2-colouring is easy.
Deciding whether two graphs are the same up to renaming vertices. It is in NP but not known to be in P or NP-complete; Babai gave a quasi-polynomial algorithm (2015, fixed 2017).

For integers N at least two and a positive bound k, ask whether N has a prime factor strictly below k. Both answers have polynomial-size checkable certificates: one factor for yes, and a complete prime factorisation with no smaller prime for no. Thus this decision problem is in NP and coNP; recovering a factorisation is a related function problem.
The decision problem "is N prime?", with input size about log₂ N bits. Long known to be in coRP via Miller–Rabin, it was proved to be in P by the AKS algorithm in 2002.
The Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena algorithm (2002), the first deterministic polynomial-time test of whether a number is prime. In practice faster randomised tests such as Miller–Rabin are used.

Optimising a linear objective subject to linear inequalities. With rational coefficients encoded in binary, linear programming has algorithms polynomial in the encoded input length; requiring variables to be integers gives NP-hard problems in general.
An algorithm that solves linear programs by shrinking an ellipsoid around the feasible region. Khachiyan used it in 1979 to prove linear programming is solvable in polynomial time.

A matching is a set of graph edges sharing no endpoints. A maximum matching has as many edges as possible and can be found in polynomial time; a perfect matching covers every vertex. These notions underlie vertex-cover algorithms and König’s theorem for bipartite graphs.
example: In the path 1–2–3–4, the edges (1, 2) and (3, 4) form a matching.

definition: Finding a minimum-length route in a graph when a finite optimum is defined, such as with nonnegative weights. The threshold decision version is in P; Dijkstra handles nonnegative weights, while Bellman–Ford also detects reachable negative cycles.
The problem: given a graph and vertices s and t, is there a path from s to t? Directed PATH is NL-complete; undirected reachability is in L (Reingold, 2005). co-PATH asks whether t is unreachable.
A vertex with no edges. It never helps cover an edge, so kernelisation for vertex cover deletes it.

A number measuring how close a graph is to a tree; every nontrivial tree has treewidth one, and an isolated vertex has treewidth zero. Many NP-hard problems become tractable at a fixed treewidth, although the dependence on that width may be very large.

A theorem that any graph property expressible in monadic second-order logic can be decided in linear time on graphs of bounded treewidth. It explains why many NP-hard problems are easy on tree-like graphs.

A dynamic program (1962) that solves TSP exactly in O(n² · 2ⁿ) time by computing the cheapest path through every subset of cities ending at each city. Still exponential, but vastly faster than checking all (n − 1)!/2 tours.
example: At 20 cities: about 4 × 10⁸ steps versus about 6 × 10¹⁶ tours.

definition: An exact search method that splits the problem into sub-problems (branch) and discards any sub-problem whose provable lower bound cannot beat the best solution found so far (bound).

Extra linear constraints added to an integer program's relaxation that remove fractional solutions without removing any integer ones, tightening the bound. Combined with branch and bound in modern solvers.
An exact TSP solver using branch and cut. In 2006 it found and proved optimal a tour of an 85,900-city instance.

Optimisation with linear constraints where some or all variables must be whole numbers; MIP means mixed-integer programming. It is NP-hard in general, but commercial and open solvers handle many large real instances.
Mathematical-optimisation solvers for linear and mixed-integer programs: Gurobi and IBM CPLEX are commercial, HiGHS is open source. They combine branch and bound, cutting planes and heuristics.
A polynomial-time algorithm with a proven guarantee on how far its answer can be from the optimum on every input. An α-approximation for a minimisation problem always returns cost at most α × OPT.
example: Taking both ends of uncovered edges is a 2-approximation for vertex cover.

definition: The worst-case factor by which an approximation algorithm's answer can differ from the optimum, often written ρ or α. A ratio of 1 means exact; vertex cover's simple algorithm has ratio 2.
The value of the best possible solution to an optimisation instance, such as the size of a minimum vertex cover. Approximation guarantees are stated relative to OPT without needing to know it.
Polynomial-time approximation scheme: for every fixed ε > 0, an algorithm within a factor 1 + ε of optimal that runs in polynomial time for that ε (the exponent may grow with 1/ε).
Fully polynomial-time approximation scheme: a PTAS whose running time is polynomial in both n and 1/ε. Knapsack has one, built by rounding values and running its pseudo-polynomial DP.

Symmetric TSP with nonnegative distances satisfying the triangle inequality. Christofides gives a factor of 1.5, and Karlin, Klein and Oveis Gharan gave a slightly better published guarantee. Approximating below 123/122 is NP-hard, so a PTAS would imply P equals NP.
TSP with arbitrary distances that need not obey the triangle inequality. No constant-factor approximation exists unless P = NP, because one could then detect Hamiltonian cycles.

The direct distance between two points is at most the sum of distances through a third point. Shortest-route distances satisfy this in the appropriate directed or undirected metric; arbitrary road-edge costs need not be symmetric or directly obey the same metric assumptions.
A 1976 algorithm for metric TSP that combines a minimum spanning tree with a minimum-weight perfect matching on odd-degree vertices, guaranteeing a tour at most 1.5 times optimal.
The algorithm that repeatedly picks the set covering the most still-uncovered elements. Its approximation ratio is the harmonic number H(n) ≤ ln n + 1, essentially the best possible unless P = NP.
H(n) = 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … + 1/n, which grows like the natural logarithm ln n. It is the approximation ratio of greedy set cover.

Every NP statement admits a polynomial-length proof checked by a polynomial-time verifier using logarithmically many random bits and reading only a constant number of proof bits. True statements have an always-accepted proof; for a false statement every proposed proof is rejected with a fixed positive probability. This gives hardness-of-approximation gaps.

Results showing that approximating a problem better than some factor is itself NP-hard (or hard under a stated conjecture), so no polynomial-time algorithm can beat that factor unless the assumption fails.
example: For any fixed positive margin, guaranteeing seven eighths plus that margin of the MAX-3SAT optimum is NP-hard.

definition: An open conjecture (Khot, 2002) that a certain labelling problem is NP-hard to approximate. If true, it pins down the exact approximability of many problems, e.g. vertex cover cannot be approximated within 2 − ε.

Fixed-parameter tractability in parameter k means a computable function of k times a polynomial in input length, with a polynomial exponent independent of k. The parameter factor may be exponential; a small parameter can help, but large graphs still incur the polynomial work.
example: The simple branching vertex-cover algorithm has an exponential factor two to the cover budget, multiplied by edge-processing work.

definition: A polynomial-time preprocessing algorithm producing an equivalent parameterised instance whose encoded size is bounded by a computable function of its parameter. For decidable parameterised problems this is equivalent to FPT; Buss’s rules give a small vertex-cover kernel.
example: Buss's rule leaves a vertex-cover instance with at most k² edges.

definition: A kernelisation rule for vertex cover: any vertex with more than k neighbours must be in every cover of size k, so take it and reduce k. Repeat with the reduced budget until no such vertex remains; a negative budget rejects. Then more than k² edges means the answer is no.

W[1]-hard means every problem in the parameterised class W[1] reduces to the target by a fixed-parameter reduction. W[1]-complete additionally requires membership in W[1]. Clique parameterised by requested size is W[1]-complete and is believed not fixed-parameter tractable.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis asserts a positive exponential rate for solving 3-SAT in the number of variables; in particular it rules out subexponential-time algorithms in that parameter. It is a conjecture stronger than P differing from NP and implies that clique has no running time consisting of a parameter-only factor times an input-size exponent sublinear in the clique size.

A practical method chosen to find useful answers, often without a claimed worst-case quality guarantee. Some methods called heuristics also have proven time or quality bounds; the label alone supplies neither.
example: Nearest-neighbour TSP tours are a common heuristic starting point.

definition: A method that repeatedly changes a current solution using nearby moves, seeking improvements. Or-opt relocates a short chain in a route; guided local search adds penalties to escape poor local optima. Locality alone does not guarantee a global optimum, though particular local-search algorithms can have proven approximation bounds.
A local-search move for TSP: remove two edges of the tour and reconnect the two paths the other way, keeping the change if the tour gets shorter.

A general strategy for guiding search, such as simulated annealing, tabu search or genetic algorithms. The label alone gives no polynomial-time worst-case quality guarantee; specific methods can have convergence theorems or guarantees under additional assumptions.
A metaheuristic that sometimes accepts worse solutions, with a probability that decreases over time, so the search can escape local optima.
A local-search metaheuristic that keeps a list of recently visited solutions or moves and forbids returning to them for a while, to avoid cycling.
A metaheuristic that evolves a population of candidate solutions by selection, recombination (crossover) and random mutation.
An imaginary black box that answers membership questions about some fixed problem in one step. Results "relative to an oracle" show which proof techniques can or cannot separate classes.
example: Baker, Gill and Solovay found oracles A and B with P^A = NP^A but P^B ≠ NP^B.

definition: A proof that two classes differ when both are given access to the same oracle. It is evidence about the unrelativised classes, not a proof.
example: Raz and Tal (2018): relative to an oracle, BQP is not contained in PH.

definition: The 1975 observation of Baker, Gill and Solovay that P vs NP has different answers relative to different oracles, so any proof technique that works equally with every oracle (like simple diagonalisation) cannot settle it.

Razborov and Rudich's 1994 barrier for a broad class of circuit lower-bound arguments called natural proofs. Strong enough lower bounds proved by these methods would contradict sufficiently secure pseudorandom function families; the barrier is conditional on those cryptographic hardness assumptions.
A barrier (Aaronson and Wigderson, 2008) extending relativisation: techniques that still work when oracles are replaced by low-degree algebraic extensions cannot resolve P vs NP either.
A function that is easy to compute but hard to invert on average for random inputs. Their existence is needed for most cryptography and would imply P ≠ NP; it is not known to follow from P ≠ NP.

A family of efficiently computable keyed functions that, with a random secret key, is computationally indistinguishable from a uniformly random function to efficient algorithms allowed to query it. The comparison preserves repeated-input answers; it does not mean fresh independent output on every call. Block ciphers are used in such roles with appropriate security bounds.
A proof that computing some function needs Boolean circuits of at least a certain size. Strong enough lower bounds would separate complexity classes; they are notoriously hard to prove.
How hard a problem is on typical inputs drawn from some distribution, rather than on its worst input. Cryptography needs average-case hardness; NP-hardness only says something about the worst case.
Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with the axiom of choice: the standard axiom system in which almost all of mathematics is formalised. Whether P vs NP could be unprovable in ZFC is an open question.

Savitch’s theorem deterministically simulates nondeterministic space using at most the square of that bound, for suitable bounds at least logarithmic in input length. It enumerates midpoint configurations recursively and reuses workspace between calls; this implies PSPACE equals NPSPACE.
example: Directed reachability on n vertices can be decided in O(log² n) space.

definition: The theorem, proved independently by Immerman and Szelepcsényi in 1987–88, that nondeterministic space classes are closed under complement for s ≥ log n. In particular NL = coNL.

The technique behind Immerman–Szelepcsényi: nondeterministically compute the exact number of vertices reachable within i steps, for i = 1, 2, …, using each count to verify the next, which lets a machine confirm a vertex is unreachable.
NL-hard means every NL problem reduces to the target through a log-space many-one reduction. NL-complete additionally requires membership in NL. Directed reachability and 2-SAT are NL-complete.

PSPACE-hard means every PSPACE problem reduces to the target by a polynomial-time many-one reduction. PSPACE-complete additionally requires membership in PSPACE; TQBF and ordinary regular-expression equivalence are examples.

EXPTIME-hard means every EXPTIME problem reduces to the target by a polynomial-time many-one reduction. EXPTIME-complete also requires membership in EXPTIME. Such complete problems are provably outside P by the time hierarchy theorem.
A Boolean formula with each variable bound by "for all" (∀) or "there exists" (∃) in front, such as ∀x ∃y (x ∨ y). A fully quantified formula is simply true or false.
example: ∀x ∃y (x ≠ y) is true: for each x, pick y = ¬x.

definition: The problem of deciding whether a fully quantified Boolean formula is true. It is PSPACE-complete (Stockmeyer and Meyer, 1973); SAT is the special case where every quantifier is "there exists".
The symbol ∀, read "for all": ∀x P(x) is true when P(x) holds for every value of x.
example: ∀x (x ∨ ¬x) is true.

definition: The symbol ∃, read "there exists": ∃x P(x) is true when P(x) holds for at least one value of x.
example: ∃x (x ∧ y) is true when y is true.

definition: Switching between ∃ and ∀ in a quantified formula. Each alternation is like a turn in a two-player game, which is why game problems land in PSPACE and why the polynomial hierarchy is built from alternations.
A two-player game on a directed graph in which players alternately extend a path without revisiting vertices; whoever cannot move loses. Deciding who wins is PSPACE-complete.

A game studied as a growing family of inputs, such as boards of varying side length, rather than one fixed finite board. Polynomial-length games with efficiently representable moves admit polynomial-space search, but PSPACE-hardness needs a separate proof. Longer game families can be EXPTIME-complete.
A two-player board game in which placed discs flip the opponent's discs they enclose. Generalised to n × n boards, deciding the winner is PSPACE-complete.
Chess on an n × n board with a suitably scaled set of pieces. Fraenkel and Lichtenstein (1981) proved deciding a winning position EXPTIME-complete, so it is provably not in P.

Go is a two-player territory game with rules restricting repetitions, including ko. Robson’s 1983 EXPTIME-completeness result concerns a specified generalised simple-ko rule variant on growing boards; complexity depends on repetition and scoring rules, so it is not a blanket theorem about every real-world ruleset.
Deciding whether two regular expressions (using union, concatenation and Kleene star) describe the same set of strings. It is PSPACE-complete; with a squaring operator it becomes EXPSPACE-complete.
The regular-expression operator *, meaning "zero or more repetitions". a* matches "", "a", "aa", and so on.
A regex feature such as \1 that must match the same text an earlier group matched. It takes regexes beyond regular languages: matching with backreferences is NP-hard.
The standard method for turning an NFA into an equivalent DFA, using one DFA state per set of NFA states. It can create up to 2ⁿ states from n NFA states.
A logic for stating properties of sequences of events over time, such as "every request is eventually granted". Checking a system model against an LTL formula is PSPACE-complete in the formula size.
Automatically checking whether a finite-state model of hardware or software satisfies a formal specification by exploring its states.

Finding a sequence of actions taking a system from a start state to a goal. Plan existence for finite propositional STRIPS, with explicitly encoded facts and ground actions, is PSPACE-complete; other planning representations require separate complexity analyses.

Stanford Research Institute Problem Solver (1971): a planning formalism whose actions have preconditions and add/delete effects on facts. With finite propositional facts and explicitly listed ground actions, deciding plan existence is PSPACE-complete (Bylander, 1994).

A language recognised by a nondeterministic Turing machine whose usable tape is linearly bounded in input length, giving nondeterministic linear space. This class is closed under complement by Immerman–Szelepcsényi. Grammar presentations conventionally treat the empty word separately.

An algorithm that makes random choices (its "coin flips") as it runs. Its error probability or running time is measured over its own coin flips for every input, with no assumption that the input is random.
A randomised algorithm that is always correct but whose running time is random. ZPP is the class of problems with expected-polynomial-time Las Vegas algorithms.
example: Randomised quicksort always sorts; only its running time varies.

definition: A randomised algorithm with a bounded running time that may give a wrong answer with small probability. Miller–Rabin may wrongly call a composite "probably prime".

Quicksort with pivots chosen uniformly and independently at recursive steps. With distinct keys and a total ordering it makes an expected number of comparisons proportional to n times log n for every fixed n-key input. Duplicate keys require suitable partitioning to keep the same bound.
Randomised polynomial time: decision problems with a polynomial-time randomised algorithm that never accepts a no-instance and accepts a yes-instance with probability at least 1/2 (one-sided error).
The complements of RP problems: yes-instances are always accepted, and no-instances are rejected with probability at least 1/2. Polynomial identity testing is in coRP.
Zero-error probabilistic polynomial time: problems solved by a randomised algorithm that is never wrong and runs in expected polynomial time. ZPP = RP ∩ coRP.

Bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time: decision problems a randomised polynomial-time algorithm answers correctly with probability at least 2/3 on every input. It is widely conjectured that BPP = P.

Probabilistic polynomial time: decision problems with a polynomial-time randomised algorithm accepting yes-instances with probability greater than one half and no-instances with probability at most one half. The acceptance gap can be exponentially small, so BPP-style efficient majority amplification is not guaranteed; BQP is contained in PP and PP in PSPACE.
Errors confined to one input type. RP never accepts a no-instance, so acceptance is certain evidence of yes; coRP never rejects a yes-instance, so rejection is certain evidence of no.
An algorithm may err on both yes- and no-instances. For BPP, the error is bounded below one half by a fixed gap on every input, so independent majority repetition reduces it exponentially.

Repeating a decision algorithm with independent trials to reduce its error: accept if any trial accepts for RP false-negative error, and accept only if all trials accept for coRP false-positive error, including Miller–Rabin. For bounded two-sided error with a success probability separated above one half by a fixed positive gap, use majority voting; the error then falls exponentially with the number of trials.
example: Twenty runs of an RP algorithm with error 1/2 give error 2⁻²⁰, below one in a million.

definition: An inequality showing that the sum of many independent random trials is exponentially unlikely to stray far from its expected value. It is why majority voting reduces BPP error exponentially.

Running an algorithm several times and outputting the answer given by more than half the runs. For BPP, with independent runs, the chance the majority is wrong falls exponentially with the number of runs.
example: With error 1/3 per run, 101 runs give a majority error of about 0.00027.

definition: A randomised check of a claimed square-matrix product using exact arithmetic over the integers or a field: choose an independent uniform 0/1 vector r and compare A(Br) with Cr. It uses quadratically many arithmetic operations per trial; a wrong product passes with probability at most one half. Floating-point rounding and bit-operation costs need separate analysis.
Multiplying an n × n matrix by a vector of length n, giving a vector; it costs about n² multiplications, far fewer than a full matrix product.
A circuit whose gates add and multiply numbers, computing a polynomial in its inputs. It can describe a polynomial compactly even when the expanded form has exponentially many terms.

Deciding whether the polynomial represented by an arithmetic circuit is identically zero. With standard effective coefficient encodings and polynomial-cost exact or modular evaluation, it is in coRP via random evaluations and Schwartz–Zippel; no general deterministic polynomial-time algorithm is known.

Over a field or integral domain, a nonzero polynomial of total degree d vanishes with probability at most d divided by the size of S when each coordinate is chosen independently and uniformly from the same finite set S of distinct domain elements.
example: A degree-10 polynomial with values from a set of 1,000 numbers is wrongly zero with probability at most 1%.

definition: The highest total power among a polynomial's terms. x²y + 3x has total degree 3.

Turning a randomised algorithm into a deterministic one with similar efficiency. The AKS primality test derandomised primality; the conjecture P = BPP says this is always possible up to polynomial cost.
The fact that the probability at least one of several events happens is at most the sum of their probabilities.
example: If each of 2ⁿ inputs fails with probability below 2⁻ⁿ, the chance any fails is below 1.

definition: Problems solvable by polynomial-size Boolean circuits, one circuit per input length; equivalently, polynomial time with a polynomial-length "advice" string that depends only on the input length. Adleman (1978) proved RP ⊆ P/poly, and Bennett and Gill (1981) extended it to BPP ⊆ P/poly, often called Adleman's theorem.

aliases: second level of the polynomial hierarchy
definition: A tower of classes generalising NP and coNP by alternating "there exists" and "for all" over polynomial-size strings. Σ₁ = NP, Π₁ = coNP; Σ₂ problems have the form ∃y ∀z R(x, y, z). If P = NP, the whole hierarchy collapses to P.
The class of problems solvable deterministically in time 2^O(n), linear in the exponent. Impagliazzo and Wigderson showed that if some problem in E needs circuits of size 2^Ω(n), then P = BPP.

Bounded-error quantum polynomial time: decision problems solved by polynomial-time-uniform polynomial-size quantum circuits with error at most one third on every input. BPP is contained in BQP, which is contained in PP and PSPACE. Shor’s factorisation function algorithm yields a BQP algorithm for the associated bounded-factor decision problem.

The basic unit of quantum information. A pure n-qubit state has two to the power n complex amplitudes; measurement of the full register in the computational basis returns one n-bit string. Physical noisy qubits and error-corrected logical qubits describe different hardware roles, not different measurement rules.
A complex number attached to each possible outcome of a quantum state. Measuring gives outcome x with probability |amplitude of x|²; amplitudes can cancel or reinforce, unlike probabilities.

Amplitudes adding together (constructive) or cancelling out (destructive). Quantum algorithms work by arranging for wrong answers' amplitudes to cancel and right answers' to reinforce, not by "trying everything in parallel".

An operation producing a classical outcome with probability given by the quantum state and updating that state according to the measured outcome. Measuring a whole pure register in the computational basis gives a bit string with probability equal to its amplitude’s squared magnitude; partial measurement can leave superposition in the unmeasured part.
A sequence of quantum gates acting on qubits, followed by measurement: the standard model for quantum algorithms and for defining BQP.

A quantum algorithm giving a square-root query bound for black-box search. With one marked item among many candidates, it uses approximately pi over four times the square root of the candidate count for high success probability; multiple marked items change the count. The bounded-error square-root scaling is optimal in the black-box model.
example: Searching 2¹²⁸ keys takes about 2⁶⁴ Grover iterations.

definition: Searching for an input that a function marks as correct when the only access is to evaluate the function (query it), with no knowledge of its structure.

The number of calls to a black-box function, ignoring other computation and the cost of implementing each call. Quantum advantages are proved in this model; this does not establish unrelativised class separations such as BQP differing from BPP, which remain open.
The 1997 result of Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard and Vazirani that any quantum algorithm for black-box search over N items needs Ω(√N) queries, so Grover's algorithm is optimal.

A leading general-purpose classical integer-factorisation method. Its usual heuristic expected running-time estimate is subexponential in the integer’s bit length, but no classical polynomial-time general factoring algorithm is known.

A public-key cryptosystem introduced by Rivest, Shamir and Adleman in 1977. Efficiently factoring its modulus enables key recovery, so factoring hardness is necessary, though it is not known to imply RSA inversion hardness. RSA-2048 uses a 2,048-bit modulus; Shor threatens it on a sufficiently large fault-tolerant quantum computer.
Cryptographic schemes believed secure against quantum computers, based on problems such as lattice problems rather than factoring or discrete logarithms.
example: NIST standardised ML-KEM in FIPS 203 in 2024.

definition: Module-Lattice-based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism, standardised by NIST as FIPS 203 in August 2024 and derived from CRYSTALS-Kyber. It lets two parties agree a shared secret key in a way believed secure against quantum attacks.
Federal Information Processing Standards: US government standards published by NIST, including cryptographic ones such as FIPS 203 (ML-KEM).

aliases: National Institute of Standards and Technology
definition: The US National Institute of Standards and Technology, which publishes widely adopted cryptographic standards and ran the post-quantum cryptography competition.

A demonstration that a quantum device performs some task much faster than known classical methods. Google's 2019 random-circuit sampling experiment was such a claim; improved classical simulations later narrowed the gap.

Cryptography where parties share a secret key, as in the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES); AES-128 and AES-256 use 128-bit and 256-bit keys respectively. In the ideal generic quantum key-search query model, Grover halves the key-length exponent, so doubling the key length restores that exponent. Physical cost, parallelism and attacks exploiting cipher structure need separate analysis.

coNP-hard means every coNP problem reduces to the target by a polynomial-time many-one reduction. coNP-complete additionally requires membership in coNP; UNSAT and TAUTOLOGY are examples. If a coNP-complete problem were in NP, NP and coNP would be equal.

Writing a number N as N copies of one symbol (5 = 11111) instead of in binary. It makes the input exponentially longer, so a pseudo-polynomial algorithm becomes polynomial in that longer input length.
example: In binary 1,000,000 takes 20 bits; in unary it takes a million symbols.

definition: A 1978 public-key cryptosystem based on a knapsack (subset-sum) problem. Although subset sum is NP-complete, the specific instances it used were easy: Shamir presented a polynomial-time attack in 1982 (journal version 1984), showing worst-case hardness is not enough for cryptography.
CNF formulas stating that n + 1 pigeons fit into n holes with no two sharing, which is impossible. Haken (1985) proved every resolution proof of their unsatisfiability is exponentially long.

APX contains optimisation problems with polynomial-time verifiable feasible solutions and a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation. Under an approximation-preserving reduction notion, APX-hard means every APX problem reduces to the target; APX-complete additionally requires membership in APX. Standard APX-hard problems such as vertex cover have no PTAS unless P equals NP.
example: Vertex cover and metric TSP are APX-hard.

definition: A reduction between optimisation problems that also carries approximation guarantees across, so a good approximation for the target gives one for the source. Ordinary Karp reductions need not do this.
The difference between a found solution's cost and a proven lower bound on the optimum, often as a percentage. It certifies how far from optimal the answer can be.
example: A 1,050 km route with a proven 1,000 km lower bound is within 5% of optimal.

definition: An easier version of an optimisation problem with some constraints dropped, such as allowing fractional values in an integer program. Its optimum is a bound on the true optimum.
Growing like a power of the logarithm, (log n)^c for a constant c. Such factors grow far more slowly than any power of n.
example: (log₂ 10⁶)² is about 400.

definition: Google's open-source operations-research toolkit, with routing, scheduling, constraint and integer-programming solvers.

A method that incrementally builds an initial feasible solution, such as nearest neighbour choosing the closest unvisited city or a savings method merging routes. It can be followed by improvement moves such as 2-opt or Or-opt; guided local search is an improvement strategy, not a construction rule.
The smallest d such that every subgraph has a vertex of degree at most d. Sparse real-world networks often have low degeneracy, which makes clique search much faster in practice.
A symbol encoding the current machine state and head position in a Cook–Levin tableau row. Other cells hold ordinary tape-alphabet symbols; state markers and tape symbols have different roles.
Omer Reingold's 2005 result that reachability in undirected graphs can be decided in deterministic logarithmic space, putting it in L.
László Babai's 2015 algorithm (corrected in 2017) solving graph isomorphism in quasi-polynomial time, the biggest advance on the problem in decades.

Håstad’s optimal inapproximability result for MAX-3SAT with three distinct variables per clause: for every fixed positive margin, a polynomial-time guarantee above seven eighths of optimum would imply P equals NP. The random-assignment expectation reaches seven eighths, and conditional expectation derandomises that guarantee.
A variable that can only be true or false (often written 1 or 0). SAT formulas are built from Boolean variables joined by AND, OR and NOT.
The 1983 theorem that BPP is contained in Σ₂ ∩ Π₂, the second level of the polynomial hierarchy. It implies that if P = NP then P = BPP.
The 1997 result that if some problem solvable in time 2^O(n) needs Boolean circuits of size 2^Ω(n), then P = BPP: hardness can be turned into pseudorandomness that removes the need for random bits.
A black-box problem (Simon, 1994) that a quantum computer solves with polynomially many queries while any classical randomised algorithm needs exponentially many. It inspired Shor’s algorithm.

The element used to partition a quicksort subproblem. Uniform random pivot choices give the standard expected comparison bound for distinct totally ordered keys; duplicate handling and adversarially changing inputs need separate analysis.
The average running time over a randomised algorithm’s own random choices, for the worst-case input. ZPP is defined by expected polynomial running time.
The finite set of symbols a Turing machine may write on its tape, written Γ (capital gamma), including the blank. Its size |Γ| is a constant fixed by the machine.
example: A machine with tape alphabet {0, 1, blank} has |Γ| = 3.

definition: One of the finitely many internal states of a Turing machine’s finite control, collected in the set Q. Together with head positions and tape contents it makes up a configuration.
An automaton that runs two automata in parallel, with one state for each pair of their states. It is used to compare languages, e.g. to search for a string accepted by one but not the other.

A sparse graph with strong connectivity quantified by expansion: each vertex set of at most half the vertices has many neighbours or edges outside it relative to its size. Reingold used expanders to put undirected reachability in logarithmic space.

A two-player connection game on a rhombus of hexagonal cells. Generalised to n × n boards, deciding whether the first player can win from a position is PSPACE-complete (Reisch, 1981; Even and Tarjan had shown the version on arbitrary graphs PSPACE-complete in 1976).
A speed-up that replaces a cost of N steps with about the square root of N. Grover's algorithm gives one for black-box search: still exponential when N = 2ⁿ, but with half the exponent.
example: Searching 2¹²⁸ keys classically takes about 2¹²⁸ tries; with Grover's quadratic speed-up it takes about 2⁶⁴ queries.

definition: The time since the Big Bang, about 13.8 billion years (roughly 1.4 × 10¹⁰ years or 4.4 × 10¹⁷ seconds) on the Planck 2018 measurements. Complexity texts use it as a yardstick for computations that can never finish.
example: 2¹⁰⁰ steps at 10⁹ steps per second take about 4 × 10¹³ years, thousands of times the age of the universe.

definition: A number system in which you can add, subtract, multiply and divide by anything except zero, with the usual rules. The rationals, the reals and the integers modulo a prime are fields; the Schwartz–Zippel lemma counts roots over one.
example: The integers modulo 7 form a field: every nonzero value, such as 3, has an inverse (3 × 5 = 15 ≡ 1 mod 7).

definition: A commutative number system with addition, subtraction and multiplication, distinct zero and one, and no zero divisors: two nonzero values never multiply to zero. Division need not be available. The integers are an example, and Schwartz–Zippel also holds over such systems.
example: In the integers, if a × b = 0 then a = 0 or b = 0; in the integers modulo 6 that fails (2 × 3 = 0), so they are not an integral domain.

definition: Three vertices with an edge joining every pair. In the SAT-to-Independent-Set construction, these edges allow at most one chosen literal occurrence from a clause.
A pair of distinct graph vertices with no edge between them. A complement graph places an edge at each such pair.

A rule for choosing moves that guarantees a win against every permitted sequence of opponent replies, from the stated position and under the stated game rules. It can require exponentially many cases to describe explicitly.
A memory bound that a machine can itself mark off using at most that order of working memory. This regularity condition is part of standard space hierarchy and simulation theorems.

One circuit for each input length, with a single efficient classical procedure producing each circuit’s description from that length. Uniformity prevents hiding uncomputable or unconstructible advice in a separate circuit for every length.

A logic that can quantify over individual objects and sets of objects, rather than arbitrary higher-arity relations. In Courcelle’s graph theorem, vertices and edges and their sets can express properties such as the existence of a vertex cover.

The property of a deterministic construction whose outputs resemble randomness to specified tests or observers. Passing statistical tests does not by itself make a generator safe for secrets. A pseudorandom generator produces a sequence from a seed, while a pseudorandom function answers queries consistently under a secret key.

Every decision problem in PSPACE can be translated into the target problem by a polynomial-time many-one reduction. This alone does not put the target in PSPACE: PSPACE-completeness additionally requires membership. Even an undecidable target can be PSPACE-hard.
